lesson.title: Two Paths from Source Code to a Running Program
lesson.summary: Compiled languages translate an entire program into machine code ahead of time before it runs, while interpreted languages translate and execute code as it runs, and understanding this difference explains why some languages feel faster while others feel more flexible.
lesson.body:
Once a program is written in a programming language, its source code still has to get turned into something the CPU can execute. There are two broad strategies for doing this, and most languages lean heavily toward one or the other. A compiler is a program that reads the entire source code of a program, translates it all the way down to machine code, and produces a standalone executable file. That executable can then be run directly by the operating system, without needing the original source code or the compiler present anymore. C, C++, and Rust are commonly compiled languages.

An interpreter takes a different approach. Instead of translating the whole program in advance, an interpreter reads and carries out the source code, or some intermediate form of it, while the program is running, translating and executing it piece by piece rather than producing a separate standalone executable ahead of time. Because there is no separate compile step producing a finished executable, you typically run an interpreted program by handing the source code straight to the interpreter every time you want to run it.

This difference has real consequences that programmers care about. Compiled programs tend to run faster once they start, because all the work of translating to machine code happened once, ahead of time, rather than being repeated during execution. Compiled languages also tend to catch a wider range of mistakes at compile time, before the program ever runs, because the compiler has to fully analyze the entire program to translate it. Interpreted languages, by contrast, are often easier to test and experiment with, since you can run a small piece of code immediately without a separate build step, and the same source code can often run unmodified on any machine that has a matching interpreter installed, which makes interpreted code more portable across different operating systems and processor types.

A useful way to see the contrast is imagining the same tiny program in each style. With a compiled language, you might run a command like gcc program.c -o program to produce an executable file called program, and then run ./program every time you want to execute it, with the translation step happening only once. With an interpreted language, you run something like python program.py directly, and each time you do, the interpreter processes the source code again before running it.

It is worth knowing that this split is not perfectly clean. Many modern languages, including Python, blend the two ideas. Python source code is first translated into an intermediate form called bytecode, a step that resembles compilation, and then that bytecode is executed by an interpreter, a step that resembles interpretation. This hybrid approach, along with why it matters for how Python actually runs your code, is the subject of the next few chapters, where you will look closely at the Python interpreter itself.
